extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers for the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and checklist for performing peer review of research software submissions to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS), including repository checks, installation/verification, documentation, and required paper sections. Focused on evaluating openness, sustainability, functionality, and scholarly significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed content of the JOSS paper
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper (compiled PDF) should only include: a list of authors and affiliations; a high-level summary describing functionality and purpose for a diverse, non-specialist audience; a clear statement of need; a description of how the software compares to other commonly-used packages; mentions of ongoing research projects using the software or recent scholarly publications enabled by it (if applicable); and a list of key references including a link to the software archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important: the paper should not include software documentation such as API functionality, which belongs in the software documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software license present and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be an OSI-approved license included in the repository; a plain-text LICENSE or COPYING file with the license contents is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable: a plain-text LICENSE or COPYING file with the contents of an OSI approved license. Not acceptable: only a phrase such as 'MIT license' in a README file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and significance (research impact / scholarly significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should verify that the software demonstrates clear research impact or credible scholarly significance and shows evidence of meaningful contribution to the research community rather than being a one-off tool for a single analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals include published research citing or using the software, adoption by other groups, integration into workflows, demonstrated performance improvements or novel capabilities, and clear potential for reuse and citation. Note: decision on scope and significance is ultimately made by JOSS editors; flag questionable submissions to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development history and open-source practice (screening gates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the software represents a sustained, collaborative effort that follows good open-source practices. Criteria in this section serve as pre-review screening gates; clear failures should be flagged to the handling editor for possible desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of clear failures: repository made public only days before submission, a commit history concentrated in a short window. If detected early, stop full review and notify editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development timeline (sustained development evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should show evidence of sustained development over time (preferably months or years) rather than rapid, recent code generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: commits distributed over 6+ months showing gradual feature development. OK: development spanning 6+ months but with bursty activity. Not acceptable: all or most commits concentrated in the last few weeks before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open development (public history and community engagement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should have been developed openly from early stages; for recently created public repositories there should be at least six months of public development history with evidence of releases/tags, public issues/pull requests, and ideally external engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: repository public from inception with documented releases and community interaction. OK: repository public 6+ months ago with evidence of ongoing development. Not acceptable: repository made public immediately before submission with limited history. Note: previously private development may be acceptable if authors demonstrate substantial effort and at least six months of public availability and use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative effort (contributors and community-driven improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit history should show contributions from multiple developers and evidence of iterative refinement through community feedback (multiple contributors, code review through pull requests, responses to issues and feature requests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: multiple developers contributing with evidence of iterative refinement (issues, pull requests, code review). OK: single author but with other evidence of community engagement in repo or paper. Not acceptable: single author with no evidence of community engagement or external use. For single-author projects, reviewers may accept paper evidence (citations/use) as substitute signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good open-source project practices (license, docs, QA, releases, community pathways)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project should demonstrate that it is a reusable, non-throwaway research software project following good practices: OSI-approved license, README and documentation, installation instructions, usage examples, API documentation, automated tests/CI, releases/tags, and clear contribution/support guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: all elements present and well-maintained. OK: core elements present (license, docs, tests, contribution guidelines). Bad (not acceptable): missing critical elements or appears to be a one-time code dump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: sufficient for reviewer understanding (README overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be sufficient documentation for the reviewer to understand the core functionality; a high-level overview of this documentation should be included in a README (or equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation should enable the reviewer to assess what the software does and how it is intended to be used; follow-up details (installation, examples, API docs) should be present in the repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation: statement of need in README/documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation should include a statement of need explaining what problems the software is designed to solve, who the target audience is, and its relation to other work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors the required paper section; the README's statement of need helps reviewers and users understand the purpose and target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Software dependencies should be clearly documented and installation should be handled by an automated procedure where possible; installation should follow package manager conventions when available for the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: software is simple to install and follows established distribution/dependency management approaches (e.g., pip-installable Python packages). OK: a list of dependencies with a script or Makefile to handle installation. Bad (not acceptable): dependencies are unclear or the installation process lacks automation. Criterion depends on maturity and language ecosystem (e.g., Fortran with Makefile may be sufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should include examples of how to use the software, ideally demonstrating real-world analysis problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples help reviewers verify functionality and help users adopt the software; include example inputs/outputs where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: API documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The software API should be documented to a suitable level so that core functions/methods are described with example inputs/outputs where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: all functions/methods documented including example inputs and outputs. OK: core API functionality documented. Bad (not acceptable): API is undocumented. Note: decision on sufficiency is largely left to reviewer discretion and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be clear guidelines for third-parties wishing to contribute, report issues, or seek support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, issue templates, or other clear support pathways is a positive signal of community-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality verification (installation and core behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to install the software and verify its core functionality as part of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reviewer cannot install or verify functionality, this should be raised in the review; provide documented steps or sample inputs that demonstrate behavior for objective checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and continuous integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are strongly encouraged to include an automated test suite covering core functionality, ideally hooked up to CI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: automated test suite with CI (GitHub Actions, CircleCI, etc.). OK: documented manual steps or sample input files to assert behavior. Bad (not acceptable): no way for the reviewer to objectively assess that the software works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper required sections (presence and substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The JOSS paper must include specific required sections beyond summary and references; reviewers should verify all required sections are present and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required sections include Statement of need, State of the field, Software design, Research impact statement, and AI usage disclosure. Each section should be substantive, not merely present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of need (required paper section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must have a clearly labeled 'Statement of need' section that clearly states what problems the software is designed to solve, identifies the target audience, and explains the software's relation to other work in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: clear problem statement, well-defined target audience, and context within the broader field. OK: addresses key elements but could be more specific. Bad (not acceptable): vague problem, unclear audience, or missing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the field (required paper section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must describe how the software compares to other commonly-used packages and provide a 'build vs. contribute' justification explaining the unique scholarly contribution and why existing alternatives are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thorough comparison with existing tools and clear justification for a new tool. OK: identifies related work and explains key differences. Bad (not acceptable): ignores similar tools or fails to justify not contributing to existing projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software design (required paper section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section explaining architectural choices, trade-offs considered, the design chosen and why, and why these choices matter for the research application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: thoughtful discussion of design decisions and implications. OK: clear explanation of architecture with some rationale. Bad (not acceptable): generic code-structure description without design reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research impact statement (required paper section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must provide evidence of either realized impact (publications using the software, evidence of external use or integration) or credible near-term significance (benchmarks demonstrating improvements, reproducible materials, community-readiness signals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence should be compelling and specific. Good: multiple citations, documented external users, or strong benchmarks with reproducible materials. OK: some evidence beyond the authors' group. Bad (not acceptable): only aspirational statements without concrete evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage disclosure (required paper section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper must include a section that transparently discloses any use of generative AI in software creation, documentation writing, or paper authoring; if no AI tools were used, this should be explicitly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: clear, specific disclosure of AI tool usage and verification methods. OK: statement that no AI tools were used or a general disclosure. Bad (not acceptable): missing section or vague/evasive language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should check whether the submitting author made a 'substantial contribution' (as indicated by commit history) and whether the full list of paper authors seems appropriate and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are responsible for deciding contributions; JOSS policy: purely financial contributions are not sufficient for authorship. If author list seems unexpectedly short or incorrect, raise it as a question during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation of prior similar work (novelty and attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that implement solutions already solved in other packages are acceptable if they meet other criteria and cite prior similar work; reviewers should point out relevant published work not yet cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of citation to relevant prior tools is a deficiency reviewers should flag; novelty alone is not required if prior work is properly acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review outcome categories and revision policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should grade submissions as one of: Accept, Minor Revisions, Major Revisions. JOSS does not require outright rejection in cases of major revisions; authors may be given as long as needed to address issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to indicate the level of changes required; editors manage final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary languages/development environments policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions relying on proprietary/closed-source languages or development environments are acceptable provided they meet other requirements and the reviewer can install and verify functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If open-source/free variants exist, reviewers may encourage authors to make software compatible with them; inability to install due to proprietary restrictions should be raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository hosting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Repositories must be hosted at locations that allow outside users to freely open issues and propose code changes (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions will not be accepted if hosted at locations where accounts must be manually approved or paid for, regardless of who controls approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using AI to generate code (policy awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS has a detailed policy describing appropriate use of AI by authors and reviewers; reviewers should consult these guidelines before starting a review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See linked JOSS AI policy for specifics; AI usage must be disclosed in the paper and its correctness verified as described in the AI usage disclosure section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review flagging for clear failures
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers find clear failures in open-source practice or development history early (e.g., repo newly public, concentrated commits), they should flag the submission to the handling editor rather than proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor can issue a desk rejection based on these pre-review screening gates; do not expend full review effort on clearly ineligible submissions.
